profile.intro: I am a professor at Kookmin University, where I study semiconductor devices and their integration into electronic systems. My research spans silicon transistors, carbon nanotube electronics, memory and neuromorphic devices, and semiconductor sensors. Within the shared S!LK laboratory, my team connects device design, fabrication and electrical characterization to questions in energy-efficient and densely integrated electronics. I joined Kookmin in 2013 following postdoctoral research at the University of California, Berkeley, and received my Ph.D. in electrical engineering from KAIST.

research.title: Advanced transistors & 3D integration
research.short: New device structures and low-temperature processes for vertically integrated electronics.
research.description: We investigate transistor structures and fabrication routes for building multiple device layers within a limited footprint. Current directions include low-temperature silicon and germanium processing, laser recrystallization and gate-all-around devices for monolithic 3D integration. The aim is to connect material quality and transistor operation with the processing constraints of vertical integration, developing building blocks for densely integrated, energy-efficient electronic systems.

research.title: Carbon nanotubes & low-dimensional electronics
research.short: From nanoscale channels to processes that support larger integrated circuits.
research.description: Carbon nanotubes and other low-dimensional semiconductors offer ways to explore electronic devices beyond conventional silicon channels. We study how material preparation, channel geometry and gate structures shape transistor behavior, with particular interest in CNT networks and wafer-scale processing. This work brings nanoscale materials together with device fabrication, seeking practical routes from individual transistors toward integrated circuits and complementary electronic platforms.

research.title: Memory & neuromorphic devices
research.short: Charge storage, device reliability and electronic elements that emulate synaptic behavior.
research.description: Our memory research examines how charge is stored, retained and controlled in semiconductor devices. Topics include the early retention behavior of vertical NAND flash and floating-gate memories made with metallic and semiconducting carbon nanotubes. In related collaborative work, CNT devices are used to emulate synaptic behavior, connecting measured device characteristics with simulations of learning systems. These studies address both information storage and alternative approaches to computation.
research.source_note: The neuromorphic university interview was available as indexed full text; the original press article was also opened at https://www.yna.co.kr/view/AKR20170323063200063 .

research.title: Semiconductor sensors
research.short: Device structures that translate small chemical and biological changes into readable signals.
research.description: Semiconductor sensors convert changes at a material surface into electrical signals. We explore how device architecture and transistor amplification can improve the readout of small responses. A silicon nanowire–MOSFET hybrid platform combines sensing and amplification using conventional semiconductor processing, with demonstrations involving pH and charged polymers. The broader interest is in connecting nanoscale sensing elements with electronic readout for biological and chemical measurement.

media.summary_en: Kookmin and Sejong researchers demonstrate CNT devices that emulate neural behavior. The report connects device characteristics with simulations of handwritten-image recognition in a neuromorphic system.
media.attribution: Joint work with Sungho Kim. Handwriting recognition was simulated; the headline's neuron count describes the human brain, not the fabricated system.

media.summary_en: A collaboration with Yang-Kyu Choi's team at KAIST explores three-dimensional fin-gate CNT transistors, using vertical geometry to increase nanotube density in devices fabricated over large areas.
media.attribution: KAIST-led collaborative work. Numerical comparisons from the newspaper headline are preserved only in the original headline, not adopted as general website claims.
